label: q2-critic
summary: Verdict: the noise-ceiling story is real but weak as the main explanation. Published noise estimates imply a ceiling of Pearson r about 0.85-0.95, above the r about 0.75-0.80 that leakage-free models reach on CASF2016, and well above the gap between leaky and clean splits. Leakage inflates scores and clean splits expose the drop (Graber 2025, Volkov 2022); a simulation with stated noise shows split choice moves r by 0.7 while noise of 0.8 log units moves it by under 0.05. Cleaner splits do not restore performance, they reveal it. Caveat: the ceiling can bind at the level of per-assay agreement (Landrum 2024) and in narrow-range datasets, and my simulation has a large label SD (2.64) which makes noise look cheap.
lay_summary: Many people say binding-prediction programs fail because the lab measurements they learn from are noisy. We checked. The noise is real, but it only caps a perfect program at a score of about 0.85 to 0.95 out of 1, while today's honest programs get about 0.75 to 0.80. The bigger problem is that benchmark tests often contain near-copies of the training examples, like a student who has seen the exam questions. In our simulated experiment, a program scored 0.90 when tested on look-alikes of what it had studied and about 0.19 on truly new proteins and molecules, and adding measurement noise barely changed that. A fairer test does not make programs better; it shows how good they really are.

findings.claim: Mean experimental error between independent ChEMBL Ki measurements is 0.44 pKi units (SD 0.54, median 0.34); max achievable squared Pearson R on large datasets estimated 0.81 (r about 0.90, my sqrt).
findings.evidence_quote: The maximum possible squared Pearson correlation coefficient (R(2)) on large data sets is estimated to be 0.81.

findings.claim: Cross-assay IC50 agreement in ChEMBL is poor: minimal curation Kendall tau 0.51, 65% of points differ >0.3 log; maximal curation tau 0.71, 48% differ >0.3 log.
findings.evidence_quote: almost 65% of the points differ by more than 0.3 log units, 27% differ by more than one log unit, and the correlation between the assays, as measured by Kendall's τ, is only 0.51.

findings.claim: Converting Landrum tau to Pearson via r=sin(pi*tau/2) (bivariate normal assumption) gives between-assay r 0.718 (minimal) and 0.898 (maximal); a perfect predictor then correlates sqrt(r) = 0.847 / 0.948 with a single assay, assuming equal reliability.

Using Kramer SD 0.54 as per-measurement noise and assumed label SD 1.4-2.2 (assumption, not sourced) gives ceiling r 0.92-0.97; if 0.54 is a pair-difference SD, per-measurement sigma is 0.38 and ceiling is higher.

Mixing public IC50 data adds only moderate noise: SD of IC50 pairs is only 25% larger than SD of Ki pairs (Kalliokoski). Disagrees in emphasis with Landrum 2024, which finds substantially poorer agreement under minimal curation.
findings.evidence_quote: The standard deviation of IC50 data is only 25% larger than the standard deviation of Ki data

findings.claim: Train-test leakage: nearly 600 PDBbind-CASF similarities involving 49% of CASF complexes.
findings.evidence_quote: nearly 600 such similarities were detected between PDBbind training and CASF complexes, involving 49% of all CASF complexes.

findings.claim: A trivial nearest-neighbour search (mean label of 5 most similar training complexes) reaches CASF2016 Pearson 0.716 on original PDBbind; ligand-only similarity search 0.707. On CleanSplit these fall to 0.653 and 0.625.
findings.evidence_quote: Averaging the affinity label of the five most similar training complexes resulted in an r.m.s.e. of 1.648 and a Pearson correlation of 0.653.

findings.claim: Trained on CleanSplit, GEMS reaches CASF2016 Pearson 0.803 (RMSE 1.308), GenScore 0.780, Pafnucy 0.746: clean-split performance is about 0.75-0.80, below the 0.85-0.95 noise ceilings, so the ceiling is not what binds on CASF. Pafnucy dropped substantially on CleanSplit, GenScore much less.
findings.evidence_quote: With a prediction r.m.s.e. of 1.308 and a Pearson correlation of 0.803, GEMS considerably outperforms Pafnucy (r.m.s.e. = 1.484, Pearson R = 0.746) and GenScore (r.m.s.e. = 1.362, Pearson R = 0.780)

findings.claim: Original-split Pafnucy retrained on PDBbind 2020 had CASF RMSE 1.046; its Pearson was in a figure/table I did not read. So the leaky-to-clean RMSE change is 1.046 -> 1.484.
findings.evidence_quote: This increased Pafnucy’s CASF performance to an r.m.s.e. of 1.046, making it the best-performing binding affinity prediction models evaluated on the complete CASF2016 dataset

findings.claim: Memorisation dominates in deep affinity models; explicit interaction description gives no advantage over ligand or protein descriptors.
findings.evidence_quote: Simple models, inferring binding affinities of test samples from that of the closest ligands or proteins in the training set, already exhibit good performances, suggesting that memorization largely dominates true learning

findings.claim: Simulation: RF on ligand+protein descriptors, noise SD 0.4 log units: r vs noisy labels 0.904 (random pair split), 0.797 (series held out), 0.581 (protein family held out), 0.200 (both held out). Split choice changes r by 0.70; noise 0 -> 0.8 changes r by at most 0.045 (random split 0.916 -> 0.871).
Simulation: reported r vs noisy labels is always at or below the ceiling and the ceiling is never binding: reported/ceiling is 0.91 under random split and 0.20 under strict split at sigma 0.4.
Simulation: a ligand-only model scores r=0.265 on random pair split, falling to -0.10 under both-held-out, illustrating that memorisable series/protein offsets, not noise, create apparent skill.

Limit of the simulation: true-value SD is 2.64 (world seed 0), larger than real pKd spreads, so noise SD 0.8 costs little; the ceiling would bind harder in narrow-range sets (e.g. a congeneric series with SD about 0.7 and noise 0.5 gives r_max about 0.82 by sqrt(1-0.25/0.49)). DGP is built by me, so it demonstrates mechanism only, not real-world magnitudes.

Better splits do not restore performance: in both the literature (CleanSplit lowers the scores of retrained models) and the simulation (held-out splits lower r). Restoration came only from model/architecture changes (GEMS 0.803 on CleanSplit per authors).
findings.evidence_quote: Retraining current top-performing models on CleanSplit caused their benchmark performance to drop substantially, indicating that the performance of existing models is largely driven by data leakage.

key_claims.claim: Published noise estimates (Kramer R2max 0.81; Landrum tau 0.51-0.71) imply a ceiling of r about 0.85-0.95, above what leakage-free models reach on CASF2016 (r 0.75-0.80); so noise is not the binding constraint on that benchmark.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The maximum possible squared Pearson correlation coefficient (R(2)) on large data sets is estimated to be 0.81.

key_claims.claim: Leakage between PDBbind and CASF inflates scores: 49% of CASF complexes have near-duplicates, and a similarity-lookup gets r 0.716 with no learning.
key_claims.evidence_quote: involving 49% of all CASF complexes. These findings reveal a clear train–test data leakage

key_claims.claim: In a controlled simulation, split type changes reported r from 0.90 to 0.20 while 0.8 log-unit label noise changes it by under 0.05.

recommendations: State the Lean claim as a conditional: reported r <= sqrt(reliability) of the labels, and note it is slack (not binding) for CASF-type benchmarks; pair it with a leakage lemma (test items with train neighbour at similarity above threshold) rather than treating ceiling as the explanation.
Always report a nearest-neighbour baseline and a ligand-only baseline next to any model; if they come within 0.1 r of the model, the split is leaky.
Use label-noise ceilings per dataset (assay-matched, Landrum maximal curation) rather than a global 0.81.
Next test: estimate the CASF2016 label SD from the data file and compute its specific ceiling (I could not do so without downloading it).
